title: You’d Have to be a Millionaire to Buy the Centenaire, the First Monegasque Supercar

body_markdown:
Monaco. Just the word makes you think of cars going fast, doesn’t it? The Grand Prix held on its streets has been running for nearly 100 years, the rally to get there has been going for 115, and Prince Albert II is a well-known car guy. Yet the 2.08 square-kilometer microstate is not known for actually *making* any cars. Not much room for an assembly line with all those penthouses and fancy restaurants, I guess.


There are a couple of low-volume Monegasque automobiles of note, though, and an example has popped up as a star consignment of Broad Arrow’s upcoming Zoute Concours Auction in Belgium. It’s obscure, it’s awesome, and, appropriately enough, it’s expensive. The presale estimate for it is €900,000–€1,200,000 (about $1.03M–$1.37M). Its name is the[Monte Carlo Automotive (MCA) Centenaire](https://www.broadarrowauctions.com/vehicles/zt26_r0078/1990-monte-carlo-automotive-centenaire) .


Broad Arrow


Broad Arrow


Broad Arrow


MCA was the brainchild of Fulvio Maria Ballabio, an Italian racing driver whose career highlights include Formula 2 and a fifth-place finish at Le Mans. In the mid-1980s, he began forming a car company in glitzy Monaco, aiming to introduce a supercar for 1990. That would be just in time for the 100th birthday of the Automobile Club de Monaco, the body that organizes the Monaco Grand Prix and Monte Carlo Rally, and the reason behind the name “Centenaire.”


Among the team he was able to assemble were former Ferrari and Alfa Romeo man Carlo Chiti, and racer Guglielmo Bellasi. The Centenaire took about five years to develop, and its most notable feature was a carbon-fiber monocoque. Such technology was still relatively fresh to Formula 1 at the time, and the MCA was indeed the first production road car with a carbon monocoque when it was first presented to Monaco’s royals in May 1990. That means it beat out the[Jaguar XJR-15](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/jaguar/xjr~15/1990/1990-jaguar-xjr~15-base?id=aCn1I000000DHzJSAW) , which often gets the credit for being the first carbon-tub road car, even though it debuted a few months later.


While MCA had a cutting-edge chassis, they didn’t have an engine, so Ballabio bought[Countach](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=lamborghini+countach) V-12s from Lamborghini. There isn’t a single stylist credited with the looks, but the proportions are standard ’90s supercar, even if they are a bit… bubbly.


Broad Arrow


When World-Champion-turned-writer Phil Hill saw the car, he concluded in *Road & Track* that “even with a populace as cosmopolitan and blasé as the Monegasques, a car as exot­ic as the Monte Carlo GTB still commands quite a crowd—whether rolling or roaring along.” Unfortunately, the early 1990s were a terrible time to introduce an expensive and exotic car, and MCA built just five examples from 1990 to ’92. The basic Centenaire concept limped on with a handful of experiments, including a 1993 Le Mans car that failed to qualify, and a Mercedes-powered car called the Méga Monte Carlo shown at the 1996 Geneva Motor Show. But by 1999, the company and the car were no more, another fascinating footnote in sports car history.


Broad Arrow’s Centenaire is represented as the first of the five cars built, used for development and presentation purposes. Finished in white over red, which happen to be Monaco’s national colors, it also has its original 5.2-liter Countach V-12 and ZF six-speed manual. The Lamborghini factory in Sant’Agata Bolognese reportedly kept it for 10 years before it was gifted to MCA’s founder Fulvio Ballabio in the early 2000s.


Repainted in blue around 2007, it was shown at Rétromobile that year. In 2014, the current, French owner bought the car and had it repainted in 2016. Today, the odometer (also borrowed from Lamborghini) reads 1560 km (969 miles), though that reading may not be accurate for a testing and development chassis.


Broad Arrow


Broad Arrow


Broad Arrow


Broad Arrow


The late ’80s to early ’90s were a golden age for upstart manufacturers looking to cash in on the supercar craze. The Centenaire is an obscure find even among that rarefied crowd, even if it does boast a groundbreaking chassis.


Unsurprisingly, we’ve never seen one of these oddballs sell before, so our guess on value is only as good as Broad Arrow’s estimate. We’ll have to wait and see what the bidders think when the Centenaire crosses the block on October 9.
